finding: 56% of responding Georgia local governments collaborate with nonprofits; counties more than cities (76.5% vs 48.2%), a difference eliminated when controlling for jurisdictional size.
quote: County governments reported higher rates of intersectoral activity than city governments (76.5 percent versus 48.2 percent); this difference was eliminated when controlling for jurisdictional size.

finding: 52% of charitable nonprofits report formal or informal collaboration with their local city or county government.
quote: Among charitable nonprofit organizations, 52 percent reported that they collaborated formally or informally with their local city or county government.

finding: Government provision of resources (grants 36.8%, equipment 28.8%) is slightly more frequent than most joint operations, but only about 10% of jurisdictions report only contracts, grants and equipment.
quote: very few jurisdictions reported only contracts, grants, and equipment provision exclusive of other activities (10.9 percent of cities, 9.7 percent of counties)

finding: Joint activity per jurisdiction is limited (mean 3.2 activities for cities, 4.3 for counties); the author reads the level as neither widespread nor deep, though the activities that occur appear frequently collaborative.
quote: the results suggest a level of intersectoral collaborative activity that is neither widespread nor deep: It involves about half of all Georgia jurisdictions and just a few joint activities within each jurisdiction.

finding: 39.7% of collaborating nonprofits report a service contract with their local city or county government.
quote: Overall, 39.7 percent of collaborating Georgia nonprofits reported a service contract with their local city or county government.

finding: Noncontractual relationships involve more information exchange, sharing of volunteers, joint recruitment and nonprofit service on public boards; contractual ones more often share staff and jointly develop policies.
quote: Noncontractual relationships involve more frequent exchange of information, sharing of volunteers, joint recruitment of staff and volunteers, and nonprofit service on a public board.

finding: Funding and equipment are provided more often with formal agreements, but 25% of noncontractual relationships still receive public funding; the author infers funding can act as a control mechanism in place of a contract.
quote: a substantial amount of public funding (25 percent) and a small amount of other resources (volunteers and equipment) still are provided outside the contracting area.

finding: Most partnerships meet Peters's definition of public-private partnership, involving material and symbolic contributions from both parties.
quote: most of these partnerships meet Peters's definition of public-private partnership by involving material and symbolic contributions from both parties

finding: Government agencies contribute financial and material resources to partnerships more frequently than nonprofits do.
quote: government agencies contribute financial and material resources such as staff and volunteers to partnership efforts more frequently than do nonprofit organizations.

where_to_check: p.147, interview (county fire chief, n=5 interviews)
finding: A fire chief explains the absence of a formal agreement with the volunteer fire department by long-standing good relationships; asking for a contract would cause offence.
quote: It's all about relationships, and we've had good relationships. Because of that you don't want to alienate them and say oh, we need a contract now. They're going to take offense.

finding: Partnerships with neither public funding nor a contract rest on verbal arrangements.
quote: There's not really an official written agreement. No, it's all verbal, and it's just, we talk and meet, swap cards.

finding: Less formal relationships are said to be more common in rural counties where people know each other and a handshake is accepted as a contract.
quote: It . . . probably happens more in your rural counties where people know the people, and a handshake . . . is accepted as a contract.

finding: Pre-existing or long-standing relationships and the nonprofit's community reputation may determine whether a partnership is initiated.
quote: The county doesn't really get involved unless [the nonprofit has] a track record.

finding: The interviews show control mechanisms that depend on local culture and norms rather than on contracts.
quote: In this world, mechanisms of control are subject to variations in local culture and norms.

finding: Local government-nonprofit collaboration is widespread across most service sectors (two-fifths or more of cities in economic development, fire, parks; counties also in senior and social services).
quote: The results suggest that local government-nonprofit collaborative activity is widespread across most service sectors.

finding: Economic development is the most active area of collaboration for 26.4% of respondents, with the highest rate of shared decision making (41%).
quote: economic development was cited by more than one-quarter (26.4 percent) of respondents as the most active area of collaboration.

finding: Public safety and emergency response partnerships are on average nearly three times as long-standing as social, human and health services partnerships (24 vs 9 years) and involve more nonprofits.
quote: public safety and emergency response partnerships are, on average, nearly three times as long-standing as those in social, human, and health services (24 years compared to 9 years).

finding: In social, human and health services 61.8% of partnerships involve formal agreements and nonprofits are most likely to lead (38.2%).
quote: 61.8 percent of social, human, and health services partnerships are likely to involve formal agreements, and nonprofit partners are most likely to lead (38.2 percent).

finding: Environment/natural resources partnerships are the most formal (83.3%) and none is reported as government-led.
quote: Partnerships in environmental action and natural resources [...] are both more formal (83.3 percent involve contracts or letters of agreement) and less dependent on governmental leadership (no respondents reported government leadership).

finding: Public safety and emergency response has the lowest share of formal agreements (27.5%) and the highest share of government decision making (77.5%).
quote: Public safety and emergency response registers the lowest dependence on formal agreements but the highest dependence on government leadership.

finding: Among the most active partnerships, 51.0% involve a formal agreement.
quote: Frequency of Formal Agreement [...] Total [...] 51.0%

finding: Decision-making authority in the most active partnerships rests mainly with local government in 52.1%, is shared fairly equally in 30.8%, and rests mainly with the lead nonprofit in 17.1%.
quote: Mainly with Local Government [...] 52.1% [...] Shared Fairly Equally [...] 30.8%

finding: About three of five partnerships rely on a lead organization (61.2%), with little variation across service areas.
quote: perhaps the least variance on the question of whether or not the partnership relies on a lead organization (where three of five respondents reported affirmatively).

finding: Noncontractual partnerships involve fewer partners, are younger and are less likely to have a designated lead agency than contractual ones (lead: 47.6% vs 71.9%).
quote: partnerships operating without contract or formal agreement are more likely to involve a limited number of partners and to be younger in age. They are also less likely to have a designated lead agency

finding: In noncontractual partnerships local government makes most decisions more often (61.4% vs 40.9%); contractual partnerships more often share decision making (42.0% vs 20.5%). Results are described as preliminary.
quote: but more likely to have local government making most of the decisions. In contrast, partnerships that rely on formal agreements [...] also [are] more dependent on shared decision making.

finding: Only 18.7% of partnerships (n=32) depend on neither a formal agreement nor government leadership; these are mostly in smaller jurisdictions and one-third in social, human, health services.
quote: In only 18.7 percent of the cases (n = 32) did respondents report partnerships that depended on neither a formal agreement nor local governmental leadership

finding: Plotting the six policy areas by formality and shared decision making shows a clear distinction among policy areas.
quote: Figure 1 helps illustrate the clear distinction among policy areas regarding the frequency of these two attributes of control and formality.
